title: Understanding Beat-to-Beat Variations of P-Wave Morphologies in Atrial Fibrillation Patients During Sinus Rhythm: A Scoping Review of Atrial Simulation Studies

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm represents the surface expression of atrial depolarization and therefore provides a noninvasive window into impulse origin, interatrial conduction pathways, regional conduction velocity, and activation synchrony ref [2], ref [14]. In patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), this signal is clinically important because sinus-rhythm P waves may already encode the presence of an abnormal atrial substrate even before overt arrhythmia recurrence or progression is apparent. The broader clinical framing of AF as a heterogeneous syndrome, rather than a single electrophysiological entity, supports interpreting P-wave variability as a potential marker of concealed differences in atrial structure and conduction behavior ref [19].

From an electrophysiological perspective, beat-to-beat variation in P-wave morphology can arise when atrial activation traverses tissue with spatially nonuniform refractoriness, anisotropic conduction, variable interatrial routing, or shifting contributions from preferential bundles. Such instability is expected to increase when the atria are remodeled by fibrosis, since fibrotic tissue disrupts continuity, slows propagation, and amplifies local conduction dispersion, all of which favor changing activation sequences from beat to beat ref [38]. Likewise, altered cell-to-cell coupling can modulate P-wave appearance; experimental evidence linking connexin40 downregulation to enhanced atrial arrhythmogenesis underscores how gap-junction remodeling may generate conduction heterogeneity relevant to sinus-rhythm ECG phenotypes ref [31].

These concepts also fit clinical observations that AF vulnerability often coexists with broader electrical disease states and patient-specific modifiers. For example, inherited channelopathic backgrounds such as Brugada syndrome can be accompanied by atrial electrophysiological abnormalities and AF susceptibility ref [45], while sex-related differences in atrial electrophysiology and AF presentation further suggest that the determinants of P-wave variability are not uniform across populations ref [48]. Accordingly, analysis of beat-to-beat P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm should be viewed not merely as signal variability, but as a plausible readout of latent substrate complexity that simulation studies aim to mechanistically disentangle ref [2], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Beat-to-beat variability of P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm can be interpreted as a surface manifestation of dynamic and spatially heterogeneous atrial activation. From a propagation standpoint, small shifts in wavefront origin, conduction velocity, anisotropy, or local delay can alter the sequence of right-to-left and superior-to-inferior atrial depolarization, thereby changing P-wave amplitude, duration, and polarity across leads ref [21], ref [25]. In patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), such variability is clinically relevant because AF is not a single uniform entity but a syndrome encompassing diverse substrates and temporal patterns, making subtle sinus-rhythm ECG changes potentially informative of underlying atrial disease ref [12].

The electrophysiological basis for this variability lies in the interaction between tissue architecture and functional properties. Structural remodelling, including fibrosis and myocyte disarray, promotes discontinuous conduction and local source–sink mismatch, while cellular remodelling and altered calcium handling modify excitability and refractoriness; both mechanisms can perturb atrial activation even before overt arrhythmia is present ref [21], ref [49]. Experimental work showing that Rac1 overexpression creates an atrial arrhythmogenic substrate through structural remodelling further supports the concept that latent substrate abnormalities may manifest during sinus rhythm as altered activation patterns rather than only as sustained AF episodes ref [24].

Accordingly, P-wave variability should not be viewed merely as measurement noise, but as a candidate marker of concealed conduction instability. Modern mapping approaches provide mechanistic support by demonstrating how localized conduction barriers, preferential pathways, and shifting breakthrough sites can generate distinct activation geometries from one beat to the next ref [25]. For simulation studies, this framework is essential: models that reproduce beat-to-beat P-wave changes are most clinically meaningful when they link observable ECG variability to specific combinations of atrial structure, propagation physics, and AF-related remodelling ref [21], ref [49], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A key electrophysiological interpretation of beat-to-beat P-wave variability in atrial fibrillation patients during sinus rhythm is that surface changes may reflect shifting activation pathways through a structurally and functionally heterogeneous atrium. Contemporary mapping studies show that atrial conduction is rarely uniform in diseased tissue; instead, local slowing, anisotropy, lines of block, and wavefront fractionation can alter the sequence by which depolarization reaches the body surface, even when the initiating rhythm remains sinus [24, 38]. In this context, variation in P-wave morphology should not be viewed only as measurement noise, but as a potential noninvasive marker of unstable conduction across an arrhythmogenic substrate [19, 24].

This interpretation is strengthened by the close link between fibrosis and atrial conduction disturbance. Fibrotic remodeling disrupts cell-to-cell coupling, promotes conduction discontinuities, and increases spatial dispersion of activation, thereby creating conditions in which small beat-to-beat differences in impulse origin or preferential pathways can produce observable P-wave variation [51]. Integrated anatomical and electrophysiological mapping frameworks further indicate that the atrial substrate is multiscale, spanning cellular uncoupling, tissue architecture, and chamber-level activation dynamics; accordingly, surface P-wave instability may be an emergent manifestation of latent substrate complexity rather than a purely electrical phenomenon in isolation [42, 51].

These considerations also explain why imaging and mapping technologies are central for clinically meaningful interpretation of sinus-rhythm P-wave variability. Noninvasive electrocardiographic imaging and related approaches aim to reconstruct activation patterns from body-surface signals, while invasive and anatomically informed mapping define the substrate responsible for conduction heterogeneity and arrhythmia maintenance [19, 24, 38]. Together, these methods support the premise that subtle beat-to-beat P-wave changes may index concealed atrial remodeling before overt arrhythmia is captured, thereby providing a mechanistic bridge between routine ECG observations and simulation studies of atrial fibrillation susceptibility [19, 42].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A clinically meaningful interpretation of beat-to-beat P-wave variability in atrial fibrillation (AF) during sinus rhythm increasingly depends on advanced mapping and imaging frameworks that can relate surface-waveform changes to underlying atrial activation patterns. Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) has been developed as a noninvasive modality for reconstructing epicardial activation, thereby offering a mechanism to connect subtle variations in P-wave morphology with shifts in atrial breakthrough sites, conduction paths, and regional delays that may not be apparent on the standard 12-lead ECG alone ref [34]. More broadly, progress in cardiac electrophysiology has emphasized that arrhythmic risk is best understood by integrating electrical phenotype, anatomy, and substrate characterization rather than relying on isolated ECG descriptors ref [37], ref [40].

Experimental mapping platforms further support this multiscale view. Optical mapping has demonstrated how small spatiotemporal differences in impulse initiation and propagation can substantially alter activation sequences, providing a mechanistic analogue for sinus-rhythm P-wave variability in diseased atria ref [43]. Parallel developments in computer simulation have shown that electrophysiological heterogeneity, anisotropic conduction, and structural perturbations can be systematically manipulated to test how latent substrate abnormalities translate into observable ECG differences ref [57]. Patient-specific volume conductor modeling extends this logic by showing that torso and atrial geometry influence the surface projection of cardiac electrical activity, which is critical when interpreting inter-beat morphological variation as either true electrophysiological change or altered manifestation of a fixed substrate ref [53].

These advances are also relevant clinically because AF may remain occult for prolonged periods, as illustrated by device-detected atrial high-rate episodes that unmask otherwise silent atrial arrhythmia burden ref [33]. In such settings, sinus-rhythm P-wave variability may represent an accessible surface marker of concealed atrial disease before overt or sustained AF is documented. Accordingly, contemporary and future electrophysiology increasingly position noninvasive imaging, simulation, and patient-specific modeling as complementary tools for identifying vulnerable atrial substrate and refining AF risk stratification beyond conventional rhythm classification alone ref [37], ref [40], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical and Electrophysiological Foundations of P-Wave Variability in Atrial Fibrillation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
From a systems-electrophysiology perspective, beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm can be understood as the surface manifestation of small fluctuations in atrial source–sink balance, activation sequence, and tissue excitability. Even when sinus activation appears clinically “normal,” modest changes in conduction velocity, anisotropy, refractory state, or interatrial breakthrough can alter the spatial summation of atrial depolarization and thereby modify P-wave amplitude, duration, and polarity across leads ref [8], ref [27], ref [34]. This conceptual framework is particularly relevant in atrial fibrillation (AF), where latent conduction abnormalities may persist between arrhythmic episodes.

These mechanisms are amplified by the multiscale nature of atrial electrophysiology. Cellular determinants such as sodium-channel availability, action-potential restitution, and electrotonic coupling shape local propagation, while tissue architecture, fiber orientation, and regional heterogeneity govern how wavefronts spread through the atria ref [24], ref [34], ref [48]. Consequently, subtle beat-to-beat variation in P-wave morphology should not be interpreted as mere noise; rather, it may indicate a dynamic substrate in which conduction safety is reduced and activation pathways are more easily perturbed, creating conditions favorable for AF initiation or recurrence ref [27], ref [48].

This is also why computational approaches are central to the field. Simulation studies provide a controlled means to isolate how specific perturbations—such as localized slowing, altered coupling, or structural discontinuities—translate into observable ECG changes, including variable P-wave patterns that may be difficult to mechanistically disentangle in vivo ref [25], ref [8]. In this survey, such models should therefore be read not simply as technical exercises, but as hypothesis-generating tools that bridge basic atrial electrophysiology and the clinical interpretation of sinus-rhythm P-wave variability in patients with AF ref [25], ref [34].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A primary determinant of beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variability in atrial fibrillation patients during sinus rhythm is structural heterogeneity of the atrial substrate. Fibrosis alters local source–sink relationships, introduces conduction slowing and discontinuity, and promotes anisotropic wavefront fragmentation; even when activation remains globally sinus, these effects can shift the relative timing and dominance of right- versus left-atrial contributions to the surface P wave from one beat to the next ref [38]. Simulation studies are particularly valuable here because they can isolate how the spatial pattern, density, and transmural distribution of fibrotic tissue reshape activation pathways and body-surface projections in three-dimensional anatomically realistic atria ref [30], ref [38].

At a finer scale, fibrotic remodeling is not only a passive barrier problem. Myofibroblast accumulation in diseased atria can modify impulse propagation through electrotonic interactions with myocytes, thereby changing excitability and local conduction reserve in a spatially nonuniform manner ref [18]. In modeling terms, this means that small beat-dependent differences in cycle length or wavefront entry can be amplified into different activation sequences across Bachmann’s bundle, septal routes, or posterior left-atrial pathways, yielding subtle but measurable P-wave shape changes ref [18], ref [30]. Thus, beat-to-beat morphology variation may emerge without overt ectopy, simply from conduction operating near a structurally determined instability threshold.

These structural mechanisms also interact with dynamic modulators. Autonomic influences can alter refractoriness, conduction velocity, and regional atrial excitability, thereby changing how a fixed fibrotic substrate is recruited on successive beats ref [33]. In AF-prone atria, the combination of fibrosis, myofibroblast-related electrical coupling, and autonomically mediated electrophysiological fluctuations provides a plausible mechanistic basis for alternating or drifting P-wave morphologies during nominal sinus rhythm ref [33], ref [18], ref [38]. Accordingly, atrial simulation studies that incorporate realistic anatomy together with microstructural remodeling are best positioned to explain why apparently small substrate perturbations can produce clinically observable beat-to-beat P-wave variability ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A second major determinant of beat-to-beat P-wave variability is dynamic heterogeneity in atrial conduction itself. Even during sinus rhythm, small beatwise changes in source–sink balance, local excitability, anisotropy, and interatrial coupling can alter the sequence by which activation exits the sinoatrial region and spreads across the atria, thereby changing the body-surface projection of atrial depolarization. Classical propagation theory predicts that modest spatial differences in conduction velocity or refractoriness can redirect wavefront curvature and favor alternate preferential pathways, especially in structurally and electrically remodeled atria relevant to AF substrates ref [21], ref [55].

Simulation studies are particularly useful here because they isolate how conduction changes at multiple scales reshape the P wave. Cell-level atrial electrophysiology models show that AF-related remodeling of ion currents and calcium handling modifies excitability and action potential restitution, which in turn affects tissue conduction stability and susceptibility to beat-to-beat activation shifts ref [49]. Broader computational frameworks further demonstrate that variability is not merely noise but an emergent property of interacting anatomical, cellular, and functional parameters; population-based and variability-aware modeling explicitly reproduce distinct activation trajectories and ECG phenotypes from small parameter perturbations ref [35], ref [7].

These mechanistic insights also motivate newer multiscale and data-driven strategies. Machine-learning-assisted surrogate models can efficiently explore high-dimensional parameter spaces to identify combinations of conduction slowing, regional heterogeneity, and pathway recruitment most likely to generate alternating P-wave morphologies ref [48]. In parallel, the long evolution of tissue modeling in cardiac electrophysiology has established the methodological basis for linking microscopic conduction properties to macroscopic electrocardiographic signatures, making simulation a central tool for explaining why AF patients in apparent sinus rhythm may still exhibit subtle beat-to-beat P-wave changes ref [55], ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A distinct source of beat-to-beat P-wave variability in AF-prone atria is short-timescale modulation of atrial activation by neurohumoral and volume-sensitive mechanisms. Simulation frameworks that perturb vagal tone, regional refractoriness, or conduction velocity are consistent with the broader literature showing that cardiac cholinergic control can materially alter arrhythmia susceptibility and activation stability, even when the dominant rhythm remains sinus [31]. More generally, neuro-cardiac regulation arising from central autonomic networks can dynamically reshape impulse initiation and propagation, providing a plausible mechanism for alternating P-wave axes or subtle morphology fluctuations across consecutive beats [47,48].

These autonomic effects are unlikely to act in isolation. In structurally remodeled atria, fibrosis increases conduction discontinuity and amplifies sensitivity to small changes in local source-sink balance, so that modest autonomic or ionic perturbations can be translated into visibly different body-surface P-wave patterns [51]. Geometry also matters: excitable media with complex boundaries and anisotropic pathways can exhibit geometry-dependent changes in wavefront curvature and preferential routes of spread, implying that even minor beatwise shifts in pacemaker exit or interatrial breakthrough may generate disproportionate morphology changes on the ECG [29].

A complementary mechanism is transient tissue hydration and cell-volume regulation. Cell swelling is known to impair impulse conduction and promote arrhythmogenic behavior through changes in intercellular coupling and excitability [50]. In atrial simulations, this concept supports a mechanistic link between fluctuating microstructural conduction reserve and intermittent changes in P-wave duration, notching, or polarity. Taken together, autonomic modulation, fibrosis-mediated conduction fragility, geometry-dependent propagation, and volume-sensitive electrophysiology provide a coherent explanation for why AF patients may display beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation during otherwise nominal sinus rhythm [29,47,48,50,51].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A distinct mechanistic class of beat-to-beat P-wave variation arises from dynamic autonomic modulation of atrial excitation. Even during nominal sinus rhythm, changes in sympathetic–parasympathetic balance can alter sinoatrial firing, intra-atrial conduction velocity, refractoriness, and the relative dominance of preferential conduction routes, thereby shifting the atrial activation sequence from one beat to the next. In simulation frameworks, this mechanism is particularly relevant because small autonomically induced changes in nodal exit site or regional conduction can be amplified at the body-surface level into measurable P-wave morphology differences. Clinical and experimental electrophysiology studies support the strong dependence of cardiac activation patterns on autonomic state and neurohumoral signaling ref [43], ref [32].

The importance of this mechanism is underscored in conditions with altered autonomic control. Patients with spinal cord injury exhibit substantial electrophysiological consequences of disrupted autonomic regulation, illustrating how changes in central and peripheral autonomic inputs can reshape cardiac electrical behavior ref [43]. Experimental chemogenetic work further shows that targeted activation of Gq signaling has major effects on cardiac electrophysiology, reinforcing the plausibility that transient fluctuations in receptor-mediated signaling can modulate atrial depolarization timing and propagation on a beat-by-beat basis ref [32]. For atrial simulations, these observations motivate incorporating variable autonomic tone not merely as a heart-rate modifier, but as a determinant of activation origin and conduction heterogeneity.

Metabolic disease provides an additional, clinically relevant pathway linking autonomic dysfunction to P-wave variability. Diabetes is associated with abnormalities in cardiac autonomic innervation and electrophysiology, and animal data indicate that these effects evolve with disease duration ref [38], ref [50]. In AF-prone atria, such time-dependent autonomic remodeling may interact with pre-existing substrate abnormalities to intermittently alter sinoatrial exit, Bachmann bundle recruitment, or left atrial breakthrough patterns, yielding subtle but recurrent beat-to-beat P-wave changes during sinus rhythm. Accordingly, simulation studies seeking mechanistic fidelity should treat autonomic modulation as a dynamic and disease-conditioned input rather than a static background parameter ref [38], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanistic Determinants of Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Morphology Variations - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final mechanistic class concerns dynamic neurohumoral and pacemaking influences that alter atrial activation from one sinus beat to the next. Variations in sympathetic–parasympathetic balance can modulate atrial refractoriness, conduction velocity, and source–sink relationships, thereby shifting the earliest activation site within or near the sinoatrial node and changing interatrial breakthrough patterns. In AF-prone atria, where structural and electrophysiological reserve is already reduced, even modest autonomic fluctuations may therefore produce visible beat-to-beat differences in P-wave polarity, width, or terminal forces rather than merely rate changes ref [17], ref [23], ref [34], ref [36].

Simulation studies are particularly useful here because they can isolate transient changes in ionic conductances or nodal exit pathways and map their consequences at the body-surface level. General computational frameworks have shown how multiscale coupling between cellular electrophysiology, anisotropic tissue propagation, and torso conduction can convert small atrial activation shifts into distinct ECG morphologies ref [51], ref [25]. Related modeling work on alternans and delay-dependent dynamics further supports the broader principle that temporally varying conduction and recovery can generate beat-specific waveform differences even without gross anatomical change ref [30].

These mechanisms should also be interpreted in light of anatomy. Variability in atrial geometry, specialized conduction bundles, and venous or septal relationships influences how a changing pacemaker focus is expressed on the surface ECG; this is a recurrent theme in both general electrophysiology texts and anatomically oriented discussions of cardiac conduction substrates ref [34], ref [52]. Accordingly, in sinus rhythm of AF patients, beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation is most plausibly viewed as an emergent phenomenon arising from the interaction of autonomic state, shifting nodal/ectopic initiation, and patient-specific atrial conduction architecture rather than from a single fixed substrate alone ref [51], ref [25], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation
subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful starting point for atrial P-wave simulation is the multiscale hierarchy that links ionic dynamics, tissue propagation, chamber anatomy, and extracardiac volume conduction. Reviews of three-dimensional cardiac modelling emphasize that model choice is dictated by the target observable: biophysical reaction–diffusion formulations are appropriate when local activation and repolarization details are essential, whereas reduced-order propagation models are often sufficient when the main endpoint is activation timing or gross waveform morphology ref [30]. For sinus-rhythm P-wave studies in atrial fibrillation populations, this distinction is important because beat-to-beat morphological variation may arise from both subtle source-level changes and from geometric or conduction heterogeneity.

At the organ scale, anatomically detailed atrial models are commonly coupled to fast propagation solvers to balance physiological realism with computational tractability. In this respect, anisotropic multi-front fast marching methods provide an efficient approximation of activation spread in fibrous atrial tissue and are attractive for large parameter sweeps, uncertainty analyses, and repeated simulations needed to probe variability across beats or subjects ref [49], ref [30]. Such frameworks can encode regional conduction anisotropy and pathway-dependent delays, but they typically abstract away action-potential morphology, which limits their ability to capture variability driven by restitution, autonomic modulation, or cellular remodelling.

When the goal shifts from atrial activation to body-surface P-wave generation, torso coupling and inverse-imaging concepts become central. Noninvasive electrocardiographic imaging and related single-beat reconstruction methods show how subject-specific geometry, electrode placement, and volume-conductor assumptions shape the mapping from cardiac sources to observed electrograms ref [55], ref [43]. Although much of this literature is ventricular-focused, the methodological lesson is directly transferable to atrial simulations: reliable interpretation of P-wave variability requires joint consideration of the atrial source model and the forward model. More recent personalization strategies further suggest that jointly tuning anatomy, conduction, and electrophysiological parameters can improve predictive fidelity, providing a template for future AF-oriented sinus-rhythm P-wave studies ref [40], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation
subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A useful way to position atrial P-wave simulation frameworks is along the multiscale chain from ionic models to tissue propagation and finally to whole-atria and torso-coupled formulations. General reviews of cardiac electrophysiology modelling emphasize that each level captures different determinants of atrial activation: cellular formulations represent action-potential shape and restitution, tissue models encode anisotropy and source–sink effects, and organ-scale models translate these properties into activation sequences that can be projected to the body surface ref [35], ref [55]. For studies of beat-to-beat P-wave variability in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) during sinus rhythm, this hierarchy is especially relevant because small cycle-to-cycle changes may originate at any of these levels and become amplified when embedded in realistic anatomy ref [7], ref [48].

At the cellular end, atrial-specific electrophysiological and calcium-handling models have been extensively used to represent AF-related remodeling, including altered refractoriness, conduction reserve, and rate dependence ref [49]. However, isolated cellular models are insufficient for P-wave morphology analysis unless they are embedded in tissue or chamber geometries, because the ECG is dominated by the spatiotemporal organization of depolarization rather than by local transmembrane dynamics alone ref [35], ref [21]. This has motivated the widespread use of monodomain or eikonal-type tissue descriptions as computationally tractable middle-ground approaches that preserve activation timing and anisotropic spread while remaining feasible for large parameter sweeps and variability analyses ref [55], ref [35].

For sinus-rhythm P-wave generation in AF cohorts, the most informative frameworks are therefore population-based, multiscale models that combine remodeled atrial cell properties, heterogeneous conduction pathways, and statistical variation across anatomy and tissue parameters ref [7], ref [48]. Such models are well suited to disentangling whether beat-to-beat morphology changes arise from shifts in sinoatrial exit, preferential interatrial conduction, or spatially localized conduction slowing. More broadly, theory on cardiac propagation underscores that geometric discontinuities, anisotropy, and conduction heterogeneity can reshape activation fronts even without sustained re-entry, making them directly pertinent to subtle P-wave variation seen in structurally and electrically remodeled atria ref [21], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation
subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A particularly important layer in the modeling hierarchy is the translation from detailed atrial excitation models to computationally efficient activation frameworks that can support repeated simulations of sinus beats and morphology variability. Fast-marching formulations approximate activation-time propagation at much lower cost than full reaction–diffusion models, making them attractive for exploring multiple ectopic or sinoatrial exit patterns, local conduction changes, and anatomy-driven differences in depolarization sequences that may modulate the P wave from beat to beat in AF-prone atria ref [16]. More broadly, multiscale electrophysiology frameworks emphasize that reduced-order tissue descriptions remain valuable when embedded within larger pipelines linking cellular properties, organ-scale activation, and observable signals ref [13], ref [42].

The credibility of such reduced or personalized frameworks depends on anchoring them to imaging and experimental measurements. Optical mapping provides high-resolution observations of activation spread and repolarization dynamics, and is therefore central for calibrating tissue-scale conduction assumptions and validating simulated activation patterns before they are projected to the body surface ref [28], ref [15]. In parallel, MRI-based anatomical reconstruction enables subject-specific atrial geometry and structural context, while integrated personalization strategies have shown that combining imaging with electrophysiological data improves prediction of activation changes under altered pacing conditions ref [15]. For AF populations during sinus rhythm, this paradigm is directly relevant because subtle alterations in conduction pathways, rather than gross rhythm change alone, may underlie beatwise P-wave morphology fluctuations.

At the final stage, noninvasive inverse and forward imaging frameworks provide the bridge from atrial activation to measurable torso potentials. Reviews of noninvasive electrophysiology imaging highlight the importance of accurate volume-conductor representations, electrode geometry, and source modeling for reconstructing or predicting chamber activity from body-surface recordings ref [19]. These methods are especially pertinent for P-wave studies because atrial signals are low amplitude and highly sensitive to errors in geometry or regularization. Consequently, comprehensive in situ and whole-heart frameworks that integrate cellular, tissue, organ, and measurement domains offer a useful conceptual template for future studies seeking to explain beat-to-beat P-wave variability in AF patients during nominal sinus rhythm ref [42], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation
subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A critical layer in P-wave simulation is the validation interface between computation and measurement. Experimental platforms such as isolated heart preparations and optical mapping provide high-resolution observations of activation timing and wavefront organization, allowing atrial conduction models to be calibrated beyond purely theoretical assumptions ref [36], ref [43], ref [57]. For studies of beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm, these data are especially valuable because they help distinguish whether morphology changes arise from altered source dynamics, conduction heterogeneity, or limitations in the forward model.

When the objective shifts from atrial activation to body-surface representation, torso coupling and inverse-imaging frameworks become central. Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) established a noninvasive paradigm for relating epicardial or atrial electrical activity to measured potentials, highlighting both the promise and ill-posedness of reconstructing cardiac sources from body-surface data ref [34]. In parallel, patient-specific volume conductor modeling has shown that torso geometry, tissue boundaries, and conductivity assignment materially affect simulated electrograms and reconstructed activation patterns ref [53]. These considerations are directly relevant to AF populations, in whom anatomical remodeling may amplify inter-beat and inter-subject differences in P-wave appearance.

Accordingly, robust simulation frameworks for sinus-rhythm P-wave analysis in AF should not rely on atrial models alone, but on experimentally informed and anatomically personalized source-to-surface pipelines. Hybrid strategies that combine computational electrophysiology with experimental assessment improve confidence in activation sequence assumptions, whereas ECGI-oriented and patient-specific conductor models improve the physiological fidelity of surface projections ref [57], ref [34], ref [53]. Such integration is likely necessary if simulations are to capture subtle beat-to-beat morphology fluctuations rather than only average P-wave trends.

subsections.section_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation
subsections.subsection_title: Computational Modeling Frameworks for Atrial Activation and Surface P-Wave Simulation - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final methodological layer relevant to P-wave studies in AF populations is model personalization under computational time constraints. Patient-specific frameworks that map electrophysiological dynamics onto moving cardiac geometries aim to preserve anatomical fidelity while enabling efficient simulation of activation patterns across individualized hearts, an important prerequisite for testing how subtle atrial substrate differences may translate into beat-to-beat P-wave changes during sinus rhythm ref [27]. Closely related volumetric approaches personalize the heart model directly from surface measurements, seeking to infer distributed activation properties rather than relying only on fixed template anatomies ref [6].

For atrial depolarization and body-surface P-wave generation, the main value of these frameworks is not only anatomical customization but also the possibility of repeated simulations across varying conduction states, ectopic origins, and inter-beat timing conditions. Broad reviews of cardiac electrophysiology simulation emphasize that such multiscale integration—from tissue propagation to observable signals—is essential when relating local conduction heterogeneity to ECG morphology ref [25], while systems-level perspectives further argue that iterative exchange between computation and experiment is necessary to constrain arrhythmogenic mechanisms in human hearts ref [8].

However, beat-to-beat variability studies also require tractable runtimes for uncertainty quantification and virtual cohort analyses. Real-time or near-real-time solvers, originally motivated by interactive training environments, illustrate how reduced-order and accelerated propagation schemes can make repeated electrophysiological computations feasible ref [33]. In the context of AF-related sinus-rhythm P-wave variability, these personalized and accelerated frameworks are therefore especially attractive as a bridge between mechanistic whole-atria models and clinically scalable simulations, although their utility ultimately depends on how well personalization captures atrial fibrosis, anisotropy, and sinoatrial-to-atrial conduction pathways ref [27], ref [6], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first strand of simulation-based evidence relevant to beat-to-beat P-wave variability in atrial fibrillation (AF) substrate characterization is methodological rather than disease-specific: it establishes how atrial activation changes are transformed into observable body-surface signals. Reviews of three-dimensional cardiac computational modelling emphasize that variability in simulated ECG waveforms can arise from differences in atrial geometry, fiber anisotropy, activation sequence, and torso coupling, even when ionic dynamics are held fixed, thereby framing P-wave morphology as an emergent multiscale marker rather than a purely local phenomenon ref [30]. This systems view is directly pertinent to AF patients in sinus rhythm, where subtle substrate-dependent shifts in interatrial conduction or regional delay may produce measurable morphology changes from one beat to the next.

A complementary body of work on electrocardiographic imaging and noninvasive inverse reconstruction further supports the plausibility of linking sinus-rhythm P-wave variability to underlying atrial substrate heterogeneity. Noninvasive electrocardiographic imaging highlights the sensitivity of reconstructed activation patterns to spatiotemporal conduction differences and demonstrates that body-surface potentials can encode fine variations in atrial depolarization pathways ref [5]. Although these studies do not always target AF-related beat-to-beat P-wave variability explicitly, they provide a mechanistic basis for interpreting changing P-wave shapes as signatures of altered activation origin, conduction detours, or localized slowing within remodeled atria ref [5], ref [30].

From a practical modelling perspective, personalization and computational efficiency are central if such hypotheses are to be tested at scale. Coupled personalization frameworks show how anatomy, activation data, and electrophysiological parameters can be jointly tuned to reproduce patient-specific electrical behavior, suggesting a route toward individualized simulation of sinus-rhythm P-wave variability in AF substrates ref [40]. In parallel, fast-marching and anisotropic multi-front methods provide reduced-order but physiologically informed approximations of activation spread, enabling rapid exploration of how conduction anisotropy and pathway perturbations alter simulated wave morphology across repeated beats ref [49], ref [30]. Together, these studies indicate that current simulation platforms are already capable of probing whether clinically observed P-wave variability reflects stable structural remodeling, dynamic conduction fluctuations, or both.

subsections.section_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central contribution of simulation studies to this topic is the explicit decomposition of beat-to-beat P-wave variability into interacting sources of uncertainty and heterogeneity. Multiscale atrial models show that even during sinus rhythm, small perturbations in cellular electrophysiology, calcium handling, anisotropic conduction, and regional activation timing can alter the spatiotemporal trajectory of atrial depolarization, thereby modifying surface P-wave morphology without requiring overt arrhythmia induction ref [49], ref [21]. This mechanistic framing is important for AF substrate characterization because it suggests that subtle P-wave instability may arise from latent remodeling that remains subclinical at the level of average ECG descriptors ref [35], ref [55].

Recent simulation frameworks have therefore shifted from single “representative” atrial models toward populations of models and variability-aware pipelines. Such approaches test whether clinically observed morphology dispersion is better explained by inter-subject anatomical diversity, intra-subject fluctuations in conduction and refractoriness, or their combination ref [7], ref [35]. In this literature, P-wave variability is typically treated as an emergent property of distributed substrate changes rather than a marker of one isolated lesion mechanism, consistent with broader principles of electric propagation in excitable tissue ref [21], ref [55].

An additional trend is the use of predictive and machine-learning-assisted surrogates to accelerate exploration of high-dimensional parameter spaces that would be prohibitive with conventional bidomain or monodomain simulations alone ref [48], ref [35]. Although these studies do not always target beat-to-beat P-wave variation as a primary endpoint, they provide the computational basis for testing AF-relevant hypotheses on how fibrosis-linked slowing, altered ionic profiles, or conduction dispersion could reproduce the magnitude and directionality of clinically observed P-wave changes during sinus rhythm ref [48], ref [49], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A third strand of the simulation literature addresses beat-to-beat P-wave variability through the interaction of atrial geometry, conduction-path selection, and patient-specific model personalization rather than through isolated ionic remodeling alone. Studies on geometry-dependent wave dynamics show that tissue shape and boundary configuration can alter activation trajectories even when baseline excitability is unchanged, implying that subtle cycle-to-cycle shifts in sinoatrial exit or interatrial breakthrough could translate into measurable P-wave morphology variation on the body surface in AF-prone atria ref [29]. This concept is reinforced by fast-marching and related reduced-order propagation frameworks, which make it feasible to test large ensembles of conduction scenarios across individualized anatomies and thus probe how small differences in pathway recruitment affect activation timing patterns relevant to P-wave morphology ref [16].

Personalized electrophysiology pipelines combining structural imaging with direct electrical measurements further strengthen this interpretation. Model calibration using MRI together with optical mapping has demonstrated that individualized conduction properties can be tuned to reproduce pacing-induced changes in activation sequence, supporting the broader idea that patient-specific anatomy and anisotropy are necessary to explain morphology shifts across beats or pacing conditions ref [15]. More general in situ human-heart modelling frameworks likewise emphasize the need to integrate cellular, tissue, and organ scales when linking localized substrate heterogeneity to whole-heart activation and ECG expression ref [42]. In the context of AF substrate characterization, these approaches suggest that beat-to-beat P-wave variability is best viewed as an emergent systems-level marker of structurally constrained conduction instability rather than as a purely stochastic surface-ECG phenomenon ref [15], ref [42].

Fibrotic remodeling provides the most clinically plausible substrate within this class of models. Simulation and review work on atrial fibrosis consistently indicate that patchy collagen deposition, anisotropic conduction slowing, and discontinuous coupling can redirect wavefronts, delay interatrial propagation, and create activation patterns that would be expected to broaden or reshape the P wave from beat to beat, especially during sinus rhythm in atria previously exposed to AF ref [51]. Although most available models were developed to study arrhythmia initiation and maintenance rather than explicit P-wave variability, they collectively reproduce the mechanistic ingredients needed for clinically observed ECG lability: geometry-sensitive propagation, individualized conduction pathways, and fibrosis-mediated source-sink mismatch ref [16], ref [29], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A distinct simulation strand relevant to beat-to-beat P-wave variability concerns the forward and inverse translation from atrial activation to body-surface signals. Although much of this work was not designed specifically around sinus-rhythm P-wave lability in AF patients, it establishes the methodological basis for testing whether small changes in atrial initiation site, conduction sequence, or regional electrophysiology can generate observable ECG differences from beat to beat. In particular, ECG imaging and related simulation frameworks show that noninvasive recovery of activation patterns is highly sensitive to geometric registration, torso conductivity assumptions, and model-based regularization, implying that apparent P-wave variability may reflect both true atrial dynamics and the filtering effects of the volume conductor ref [34], ref [53], ref [57].

This has two implications for AF substrate characterization. First, patient-specific volume conductor models indicate that individualized anatomy materially alters the mapping between atrial depolarization and surface-wave morphology, so inter-beat P-wave changes should not be interpreted independently of torso-heart geometry and lead configuration ref [53]. Second, computational studies of cardiac electrophysiology more broadly have shown that regional heterogeneity can destabilize activation patterns and reshape far-field signals, supporting the hypothesis that subtle AF-related heterogeneities in atrial tissue could produce morphology fluctuations even during nominal sinus rhythm ref [8], ref [57]. While ref [8] is ventricular in focus, its central mechanistic lesson—that spatially distributed electrophysiological differences amplify waveform-level manifestations of propagation instability—remains conceptually transferable to atrial simulations.

A related body of work on rotor and activation mapping further underscores that robust identification of underlying sources requires methods that tolerate noise, incomplete sampling, and rapid spatiotemporal transitions ref [49]. For the present topic, this suggests that future atrial simulations aimed at reproducing clinically observed beat-to-beat P-wave changes should combine patient-specific forward models with uncertainty-aware inverse reconstruction, rather than treating a single simulated activation sequence as definitive ref [34], ref [49], ref [53]. Overall, current simulation evidence supports the plausibility of P-wave variability as a composite marker of substrate heterogeneity, activation-pathway shifts, and observation-model distortion, but direct AF-specific validation in sinus rhythm remains limited ref [34], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation-Based Evidence on P-Wave Variability in AF Substrate Characterization - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final theme in the simulation literature concerns translational personalization: how patient-specific geometric and surface-data constraints can be used to project atrial activation onto ECG-observable signals. Although these studies are not focused exclusively on sinus-rhythm P-wave beat-to-beat variability in AF cohorts, they provide the methodological backbone for testing whether subtle changes in activation origin, conduction velocity, chamber motion, or atrial anatomy can plausibly generate morphology fluctuations similar to those seen clinically. Dynamic patient-specific mapping frameworks and volumetric prediction approaches are especially relevant because they explicitly connect subject anatomy, moving-heart representations, and simulated electrophysiology to externally measurable electrical signatures ref [27], ref [6].

Within this framework, simulations support the view that apparent P-wave variability need not imply large changes in gross atrial anatomy; instead, modest perturbations in excitation timing, anisotropic propagation, or electromechanical state may be sufficient to alter surface morphology from one beat to the next. More general reviews of cardiac electrophysiology simulation and experiment-computation iteration have repeatedly emphasized that ECG features emerge from multiscale interactions among tissue properties, geometry, and boundary conditions, which is directly pertinent when interpreting sinus-rhythm P-wave lability as a marker of latent AF substrate rather than noise alone ref [8], ref [25].

An important practical implication is computational feasibility. If beat-specific P-wave analysis is to become useful for AF substrate characterization, simulation pipelines must eventually support rapid or near-real-time personalization and repeated scenario testing. Work on accelerated and real-time electrophysiology solvers suggests that such use is becoming technically plausible, enabling systematic exploration of how small patient-specific perturbations propagate to distinct ECG morphologies ref [33], ref [27], ref [6]. Thus, even when current models do not yet fully reproduce the full spectrum of clinically observed beat-to-beat P-wave changes, they already establish a credible mechanistic bridge between individualized atrial substrate hypotheses and observable sinus-rhythm ECG variability ref [8], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first requirement in beat-to-beat P-wave assessment is to define variability at several linked levels: body-surface waveform morphology, inferred atrial activation sequence, and underlying model state. Reviews of noninvasive electrocardiographic imaging emphasize that morphology should not be reduced to a single duration or amplitude descriptor, because small changes in activation origin, conduction anisotropy, or regional delay can alter the full spatiotemporal P-wave profile across leads ref [55]. Accordingly, simulation studies typically quantify variability using multilead descriptors such as onset-to-offset timing, peak amplitude, area, interlead correlation, template-matching error, and beat-wise dispersion of activation times on the atrial surface ref [30], ref [43].

For scoping review synthesis, it is useful to separate direct observables from model-derived metrics. Direct observables include beat-wise P-wave duration, polarity changes, axis surrogates, and waveform similarity indices, whereas model-derived quantities include local activation time maps, conduction velocity fields, and front curvature or wavefront collision measures ref [49], ref [30]. Optical mapping methodology is informative here because it formalizes how activation and recovery features should be extracted, denoised, and spatially summarized before any variability statistics are reported; analogous discipline is needed when translating simulated atrial activity into synthetic ECG features ref [57]. Likewise, methodological critiques from phase-mapping studies warn that unstable preprocessing, phase assignment, or interpolation can create apparent beat-to-beat complexity that reflects analysis choices rather than atrial dynamics ref [56].

Validation strategies therefore need to test both physiological plausibility and measurement robustness. Personalized modelling work shows the value of comparing simulated signals against independent data streams, calibrating uncertain parameters, and reporting sensitivity to anatomy, conduction properties, and observation noise ref [40]. In parallel, single-beat imaging studies demonstrate that clinically meaningful activation reconstruction can be attempted on a beat-wise basis, but only if geometric registration, forward modelling, and inverse-solution assumptions are carefully controlled ref [43], ref [55]. For this review, a practical framework is to catalogue whether studies report repeatability across beats, agreement between signal- and map-level metrics, and uncertainty propagation from preprocessing to final P-wave variability estimates ref [57], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central issue in beat-to-beat P-wave assessment is how variability is quantified across model realizations rather than from a single nominal atrial substrate. Population-based and diversity-oriented simulation frameworks argue for describing dispersion in activation and waveform outputs using distributions, confidence intervals, and sensitivity analyses, because morphology changes may arise from coupled variation in cellular kinetics, tissue conduction, and anatomy rather than measurement noise alone ref [70], ref [35]. For a scoping review, this implies that studies should report not only mean P-wave metrics, but also variability descriptors across beats, parameter sets, and virtual subjects.

Validation strategies should likewise move beyond visual agreement. Comparative modelling work has shown the value of benchmark-style cross-model evaluation, standardized stimulation conditions, and quantitative error summaries when judging whether simulated electrophysiological behavior is reproducible and interpretable ref [33], ref [51]. Historical overviews of tissue models and modern atrial cell modelling further emphasize that fidelity depends on matching the scale of validation to the scale of inference, from ion-channel and calcium-handling dynamics to tissue-level propagation relevant for atrial depolarization ref [55], ref [49]. In practice, beat-to-beat P-wave studies benefit from validation pipelines that separate feature extraction error, model-form uncertainty, and biological variability.

Emerging analytics can strengthen this pipeline. Open-source mapping and signal-processing environments facilitate reproducible extraction of spatiotemporal descriptors from high-dimensional electrophysiology data ref [36], while machine-learning and predictive-modelling approaches enable dimensionality reduction, surrogate modelling, and uncertainty-aware classification of waveform phenotypes ref [48]. Within simulation studies, these tools are particularly useful for linking latent atrial substrate properties to observable P-wave variability and for identifying which quantified features remain stable across modelling assumptions ref [35], ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A critical issue in beat-to-beat P-wave assessment is validation: simulation-derived variability metrics must be anchored to experimental or clinical observables through multi-level acquisition pipelines. Optical mapping remains central because it provides high-resolution spatiotemporal activation data that can be related to atrial depolarization timing, wavefront direction, and conduction heterogeneity, all of which shape P-wave morphology from beat to beat ref [28], ref [43]. More comprehensive in situ and whole-heart electrophysiology frameworks further support cross-scale validation by linking cellular dynamics, tissue conduction, and chamber-level activation patterns to measurable surface signatures ref [42].

For personalized models, validation strategies increasingly combine structural imaging with electrophysiological measurements. MRI-constrained geometries and optical mapping data can be assimilated to tune conduction properties and activation sequences, providing a principled basis for testing whether simulated changes in atrial excitation reproduce observed morphology shifts under altered pacing or loading conditions ref [15]. Fast-marching formulations are also useful in this context because they enable efficient generation of activation maps across parameter sets, facilitating sensitivity analysis and repeatability testing when many beats or pacing scenarios must be screened ref [16].

Translation to clinically meaningful benchmarks depends on inverse and image-based electrophysiology methods. Noninvasive imaging approaches and combined epicardial-endocardial mapping systems illustrate how reconstructed activation patterns can be compared against body-surface signals, thereby creating validation pathways for morphology-based biomarkers derived from serial P waves ref [19], ref [53]. Even algorithm-development work in small-animal ECG analysis is informative here, since it emphasizes standardized preprocessing, fiducial delineation, and reproducibility checks that are equally necessary when quantifying subtle beat-to-beat atrial waveform changes in human datasets ref [57]. Collectively, these strategies argue for validation pipelines that integrate signal-level agreement, activation-map concordance, and model-to-measurement uncertainty analysis rather than relying on visual waveform similarity alone ref [19], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A critical analytical issue in beat-to-beat P-wave assessment is how simulation-derived atrial activation patterns are validated against spatially resolved reference data rather than against scalar ECG summaries alone. Optical mapping and experimental-computational comparison studies provide an important benchmark because they quantify activation timing, wavefront trajectories, and repolarization-related signal distortions at high spatiotemporal resolution, thereby clarifying which portions of observed variability are physiological and which arise from acquisition or processing choices ref [43], ref [57]. For scoping purposes, studies should therefore be differentiated according to whether validation is limited to waveform resemblance, extended to activation-map agreement, or anchored in multimodal experimental datasets.

A second layer of rigor concerns inverse and image-based reconstruction pipelines. ECGI frameworks show that noninvasive recovery of atrial electrical activity is highly dependent on geometric accuracy, torso-heart registration, and the conditioning of the inverse problem; accordingly, apparent beat-to-beat changes in P-wave morphology may reflect reconstruction instability if these factors are not controlled ref [34], ref [53]. Patient-specific volume conductor modeling is especially relevant when comparing simulated and clinical signals, because differences in torso conductivity or atrial orientation can alter body-surface P-wave amplitude, polarity, and dispersion even when underlying atrial sources are similar ref [53]. Thus, validation pipelines in this field should explicitly separate source-level variability from transfer-to-body-surface effects.

Finally, advanced mapping analytics must be interpreted cautiously. Reviews of three-dimensional mapping emphasize that color scales, interpolation choices, and projection schemes can materially influence electrophysiological interpretation, which is directly relevant when qualitative map inspection is used to explain P-wave fluctuations ref [56]. Likewise, robust rotor-mapping methodology illustrates the broader principle that analytical outputs should be stress-tested against noise, sparse sampling, and algorithmic assumptions before being linked to mechanistic claims ref [49]. In a scoping review, this motivates extraction of not only the reported variability metrics but also the full analytical context: map construction, uncertainty handling, and sensitivity analyses ref [49], ref [56], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Quantification, Validation, and Analytical Strategies for Beat-to-Beat P-Wave Assessment - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
An important emerging direction for beat-to-beat P-wave assessment is the formalization of analysis pipelines so that variability measures can be compared across simulation studies and, ultimately, aligned with clinical datasets. Ontological resources such as ICEPO support standardized description of ionic mechanisms, model entities, and electrophysiological observables, which is valuable when different atrial simulations operationalize P-wave morphology through heterogeneous intermediate variables ref [21]. More broadly, computational electrophysiology frameworks emphasize that reproducible interpretation depends on explicit links between cellular assumptions, tissue conduction, and body-surface manifestations, rather than on isolated waveform descriptors alone ref [25], ref [76].

Validation strategies are also becoming more model-aware. Patient-specific mapping and volumetric prediction approaches suggest a pipeline in which simulated atrial activation is constrained by anatomy and surface data, then evaluated against observable signal patterns, offering a template for testing whether simulated beat-to-beat P-wave dispersion is physiologically plausible ref [75], ref [49]. Real-time and reduced-order implementations further indicate that repeated perturbation, sensitivity testing, and interactive parameter exploration are feasible, which is useful for distinguishing robust morphology variation from numerical or preprocessing artifacts ref [33].

Finally, analytical strategies are expanding beyond conventional summary statistics toward dynamical and formal methods. Studies using delay differential equations to induce alternans illustrate how temporal instability can be generated and quantified mechanistically, providing a conceptual basis for examining whether successive P-wave changes reflect true atrial dynamical transitions rather than noise ref [30]. In parallel, robust temporal-logic semantics offer a principled language for specifying waveform behaviors and tolerance bounds across time, which could support rule-based validation of beat-to-beat P-wave variability in synthetic and clinical signal sets ref [40]. Together, these developments favor review frameworks that treat quantification, validation, and interpretation as a single integrated methodological stack ref [76], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A key translational implication of atrial simulation studies is that beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm may become a noninvasive surrogate of latent atrial substrate, rather than being interpreted as noise alone. In particular, models that couple atrial anatomy, conduction heterogeneity, and body-surface forward calculations support the idea that subtle changes in activation sequence can be projected onto measurable P-wave morphology fluctuations, creating a bridge between mechanistic simulation and clinically scalable ECG phenotyping ref [53], ref [30]. This framework is especially relevant for early AF risk stratification, where fibrosis-driven conduction discontinuities are likely to amplify interbeat variability before overt arrhythmia becomes manifest ref [38].

However, important knowledge gaps remain regarding what proportion of P-wave variability reflects structural remodeling versus functional modulation. Autonomic tone is a major unresolved confounder and mediator, because neural inputs can alter atrial refractoriness, conduction, and trigger propensity on short time scales that are directly compatible with beat-to-beat P-wave changes ref [33]. Likewise, sex-related electrophysiological differences may influence atrial conduction patterns and therefore the baseline and pathological ranges of P-wave variability, yet these factors are rarely incorporated into current atrial simulations or ECG-based AF screening paradigms ref [48].

Future work should prioritize personalized and multimodal validation pipelines. Personalization strategies developed in other arrhythmia contexts show that coupling imaging, electrophysiology, and model calibration can improve patient-specific inference and may be adapted to atrial substrate assessment ref [40]. At the same time, rigorous validation will require methodological caution: mapping studies have highlighted how signal processing choices can distort inferred activation patterns, and optical mapping literature provides concrete standards for preprocessing, noise handling, and uncertainty control that are directly relevant for benchmarking simulation outputs ref [56], ref [57]. Ultimately, combining ECGI-enabled noninvasive inverse imaging with standardized computational workflows may clarify which P-wave features are robust, reproducible, and clinically actionable ref [53].

subsections.section_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central translational challenge is how to make beat-to-beat P-wave variability analyses robust enough for clinical stratification while preserving mechanistic interpretability. Atrial simulation studies indicate that small changes in cellular excitability, conduction velocity, anisotropy, and wavefront collision can produce appreciable differences in activation patterns that may project to the surface ECG as subtle P-wave morphology fluctuations, even during sinus rhythm ref [21], ref [49], ref [55]. This supports the clinical premise that repeated P-wave assessment may reveal latent atrial vulnerability, but it also underscores that morphology variation is not a one-to-one surrogate of any single substrate feature.

A major knowledge gap is model fidelity across scales. Cellular models must better capture atrial-specific electrophysiology and calcium handling, whereas tissue and organ models must represent realistic structural heterogeneity, fiber architecture, and inter-subject variability ref [49], ref [58], ref [70]. More broadly, computational electrophysiology frameworks have shown that conclusions can depend strongly on modelling assumptions, parameter choices, and calibration strategy ref [35], ref [55]. Future studies should therefore move beyond single “representative” atrial models toward population-based, uncertainty-aware pipelines that test whether simulated P-wave variability signatures remain stable across plausible biological variability ref [70], ref [35].

Methodologically, there is increasing opportunity to couple mechanistic simulation with machine learning for parameter inference, emulator construction, and phenotype discovery, provided that predictive performance does not come at the expense of physiological plausibility ref [48]. Dynamic protocol design and optimization-based model calibration may further improve identifiability of ionic and conduction determinants relevant to sinus-rhythm P-wave dynamics ref [58]. The next phase of research should thus focus on multiscale, personalized, and diversity-aware atrial models that can be prospectively linked to ECG datasets and AF outcomes, enabling simulation-derived P-wave biomarkers to become clinically actionable rather than merely descriptive ref [48], ref [35], ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A key translational priority is tighter integration of beat-to-beat P-wave analysis with imaging and mapping pipelines that can localize the atrial substrate underlying subtle sinus-rhythm abnormalities. Contemporary advances in electroanatomic mapping, noninvasive electrophysiology imaging, and multimodal anatomic imaging suggest that surface P-wave variability could be interpreted not merely as a statistical marker, but as a window into spatially heterogeneous conduction, anisotropy, and localized conduction delay across the atria ref [17], ref [19], ref [24], ref [38]. In this framework, simulation studies are especially valuable because they can explicitly test how regional conduction disturbances or altered activation pathways project onto clinically observable, low-amplitude beat-to-beat P-wave morphology changes.

However, an important knowledge gap is the limited personalization and validation of atrial models against patient-specific structural data. Work combining MRI with electrophysiological measurements has demonstrated the feasibility of personalized cardiac modeling, but analogous atrial pipelines remain insufficiently standardized for sinus-rhythm P-wave applications ref [15]. This limitation is particularly relevant in AF-prone patients, where fibrosis and other structural remodeling processes alter conduction at multiple spatial scales and may generate morphology variability even before overt arrhythmia manifests ref [51]. Future studies should therefore link atrial geometry, fibrosis burden, activation maps, and serial ECG recordings in the same individuals, enabling direct testing of whether simulated beat-to-beat P-wave fluctuations track latent substrate progression.

A further translational direction is to embed these personalized atrial simulations within broader multiscale frameworks that can evaluate intervention effects, including pharmacological modulation and substrate-guided ablation planning. Multiscale cardiac modeling has already shown value for predicting proarrhythmic drug responses, and similar strategies could be adapted to ask whether therapies reduce or amplify sinus-rhythm P-wave instability in AF-susceptible atria ref [13]. Realizing this goal will require closer coupling between in situ human electrophysiology platforms, advanced mapping technologies, and computational inference methods so that model outputs become interpretable, reproducible, and clinically actionable rather than purely descriptive ref [42], ref [24], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A key translational frontier is the integration of beat-to-beat P-wave simulation with clinically available imaging and mapping pipelines. Cardiac CT and MRI already provide anatomically detailed information for electrophysiology procedures, including chamber geometry, venous anatomy, wall thickness, and fibrosis-related substrate characterization, making them natural inputs for patient-specific atrial models that aim to explain subtle sinus-rhythm P-wave variability in AF-prone patients [ref 17, ref 55]. In parallel, the broader evolution of arrhythmia ablation toward image-informed, substrate-targeted intervention suggests that mechanistically grounded P-wave markers could eventually support pre-procedural phenotyping, risk stratification, and post-ablation surveillance rather than serving only as descriptive ECG features [ref 3, ref 37].

Noninvasive electrocardiographic imaging and related inverse approaches further strengthen this translational pathway because they offer a means to connect body-surface P-wave morphology with underlying atrial activation dynamics [ref 34, ref 53]. For sinus-rhythm applications, however, an important knowledge gap remains: current frameworks are much better developed for overt arrhythmia mapping than for resolving small beat-to-beat atrial conduction fluctuations that may precede AF. This limitation is compounded by uncertainty in torso conductivity, atrial wall representation, and registration between imaging, electrograms, and surface ECGs, all of which can alter simulated P-wave morphology and reduce clinical interpretability [ref 53, ref 57].

Future work should therefore prioritize end-to-end validation studies in which CT/MRI-derived atrial models, body-surface recordings, and invasive or noninvasive activation maps are acquired in the same patients and compared across repeated sinus beats [ref 17, ref 34, ref 55]. Such studies should test whether modeled P-wave variability identifies latent conduction heterogeneity, structural remodeling, or ablation-relevant substrate beyond conventional ECG metrics. More broadly, progress will depend on simulation platforms that are computationally efficient, experimentally benchmarked, and embedded within next-generation electrophysiology workflows envisaged for the field [ref 37, ref 57].

subsections.section_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Translational Implications, Knowledge Gaps, and Future Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major future direction is the construction of interoperable, patient-specific digital atrial models that can translate beat-to-beat P-wave variability into clinically actionable AF risk descriptors. Work on dynamic patient-specific mapping and volumetric prediction shows that electrophysiological states can be projected onto individualized heart geometries from limited surface information, supporting a path toward personalized interpretation of subtle sinus-rhythm P-wave fluctuations rather than population-average descriptors alone [ref 4, ref 6]. More broadly, iterative integration of computation and experiment remains essential if simulated P-wave morphology changes are to be trusted as mechanistic surrogates for atrial conduction heterogeneity and latent arrhythmogenic substrate [ref 8, ref 25].

However, several knowledge gaps still limit translation. First, model inputs and outputs remain insufficiently standardized across scales, making it difficult to compare ionic, tissue, and whole-heart determinants of P-wave morphology between studies; ontology-based frameworks such as ICEPO offer an important route toward harmonized nomenclature and data annotation [ref 21]. Second, present pipelines are often too slow for repeated uncertainty quantification or bedside deployment, although progress in real-time electrophysiology computation suggests that interactive or near-real-time simulation-assisted decision support is becoming technically plausible [ref 33]. These infrastructure issues are especially relevant for scoping review findings, because apparent beat-to-beat variability may otherwise reflect differences in parameterization and reporting rather than true atrial biology [ref 25, ref 8].

Looking forward, translational expansion should also include modalities and biological layers that are still underrepresented in atrial simulation studies. Cardiac optogenetics offers a powerful experimental-computational platform for causally probing conduction pathways and validating model-predicted activation patterns under controlled perturbations [ref 38]. In parallel, genotype-informed frameworks such as ablatogenomics highlight the need to connect inherited substrate, remodeling propensity, and ablation response with simulation-derived P-wave phenotypes [ref 42]. Together, these directions suggest that the next generation of studies should combine standardized ontologies, fast personalized modeling, perturbational validation, and genomic stratification to determine whether sinus-rhythm P-wave variability can become a robust biomarker for AF screening, phenotyping, and treatment selection [ref 21, ref 33, ref 42].
